short: The mind that receives, coordinates and desires — restless by nature.
beginner: Manas is the everyday thinking-feeling mind: it takes in what the senses report, wants things and wavers. Indian philosophy treats it as an instrument we have, not as who we are.
what: In Sankhya and Vedanta, manas is one of the inner instruments (antahkarana), alongside intellect (buddhi) and ego (ahankara); it coordinates the senses and generates doubt and desire. In Nyaya-Vaisheshika, manas is an atomic substance whose contact with the self and senses makes cognition possible one at a time. The Gita's Arjuna calls the mind as hard to control as the wind; Krishna answers that practice and dispassion restrain it.
scholar: Classic analyses: manas as 'samkalpa-vikalpa' (proposing and doubting) function; the Nyaya argument for atomic manas from the non-simultaneity of cognitions. Buddhist Abhidharma treats mano as the sixth sense base; Yogacara adds manas as the defiled mind that grasps at self. The Katha Upanishad's chariot image makes the mind the reins.

perspectives.view: Manas is an evolute of prakriti — material, not conscious — coordinating the senses and forming intentions.
The mind is an atomic, eternal substance; because it can join only one sense at a time, we have one cognition at a time.
The mind is part of the subtle body and an object of awareness; it is not the Self, whose light it borrows.
Mind is the sixth sense base; in Yogacara a distinct defiled mind (manas) constantly grasps at a self.
The mind (man) is restless and ego-driven, but when attuned to the Name it can itself become a place of divine light.

follow.note: The chariot image: the mind as the reins of the senses.
